title: Tiered SLO probing: latency vs cost snapshot
content:
Purpose:
Quick internal sketch to compare three practical SLO tiers (interactive, standard, background) under two workload shapes (microburst and sustained) and show how routing/batching knobs shift the cost vs latency frontier. This is a working artifact for console/rollouts folks + product optimize — not final benchmarking sweeps.

Background/context:
- Motivation: customers ask for predictable latency bands per SaaS tier. We need a concise collateral piece that shows tradeoffs and the primary levers (batching window, prewarm fraction, kv-cache hit, quantization profile).
- This doc uses synthetic session shapes derived from sessionizer traces (sampled) and a small in-house microbench harness (PR linked above). Numbers are coarse — treat as directional.

Test matrix (high level):
- SLO tiers: interactive (p90  <= 150ms target), standard (p90 <= 400ms), background (p90 <= 1s)
- Workload shapes: microburst (spiky, 90% of traffic in 10% of time), sustained (steady QPS with low variance)
- Knobs: batching window (0ms, 10ms, 50ms), prewarm fraction (0%, 25%, 75%), kv-cache hit (10%, 50%, 90%), quant profile (fp16, int8-opt)

Summary findings (short):
1) For interactive SLO, the dominant cost for microburst shapes is reserve/prewarm overhead: lowering p90 from ~220ms -> ~140ms required ~2.2x baseline reserved GPU capacity for the burst window. Cost increase: ~1.9x $/k tokens after amortizing reserved costs.
2) For standard SLO, batching (10–50ms window) amortizes well on sustained workloads: p90 stays inside target while $/k tokens drops ~30% compared to zero-batching for the same throughput.
3) kv-cache hit rates are multiplicative on both latency and cost — a shift from 10% -> 50% hit reduces median latency by ~35% and $/k by ~25% in our sweep.
4) Quantization helps cost but creates larger p99 tails for microbursts unless paired with higher prewarm. Int8-opt lowered per-token runtime by ~22% but increased p99 by ~15–30ms in spike conditions.

Example numbers (representative snapshot):
(Columns: scenario | p50 (ms) | p90 (ms) | p99 (ms) | $/k tokens)

Interactive / microburst / no-batching / prewarm 75% / kv 10% / fp16
- p50: 80 ms | p90: 220 ms | p99: 620 ms | $/k: $4.10

Interactive / microburst / small-batching 10ms / prewarm 75% / kv 50% / fp16
- p50: 70 ms | p90: 140 ms | p99: 350 ms | $/k: $3.85

Standard / sustained / batching 50ms / prewarm 25% / kv 50% / int8-opt
- p50: 95 ms | p90: 280 ms | p99: 520 ms | $/k: $2.40

Background / sustained / batching 50ms / prewarm 0% / kv 90% / int8-opt
- p50: 110 ms | p90: 680 ms | p99: 1,200 ms | $/k: $1.45

Simple ASCII frontier sketch (cost vs latency; lower-left is better):
- Legend: '*' = config points (interactive=squares, standard=circles, background=triangles)

Cost ($/k) ->   4.5 | *I1       *I2
                    |       .        
                    |       .        oS1
                  3 |    *I3  .   oS2
                    |      .
                    |   t
                  2 |     oS3      ^B1
                    |        ^B2

                  1 |        ^B3
                    +--------------------------- Latency (p90 ms)
                      100   200   300   500   800

(Interpretation: interactive configs cluster higher cost but lower p90; background is very cheap but far right on p90.)

Key lever breakdown (short notes):
- Prewarm/reserve fraction: best for microbursts where p99 is dominated by cold-starts and queuing jitter. Prewarming 50–75% is expensive but gives predictable p90/p99.
- Batching window: sweet spot at 10–30ms for standard workloads; beyond 50ms starts to violate interactive SLOs but saves more $ in sustained conditions.
- KV cache: a high hit rate is the cheapest path to both lower latency and cost. Investment in session-affinity routing + small local cache yields multiplicative wins.
- Quantization: good cost win for bulk queries; must be paired with fallback fast-paths for critical tiers.

Design implications for console/rollouts:
- Expose a "SLO profile" preset that maps to a baseline knob set: interactive = {prewarm: 75%, batch_window: 10ms, kv_target: 50%}, standard = {prewarm: 25%, batch_window: 30ms, kv_target: 50%}, background = {prewarm: 0%, batch_window: 50ms, kv_target: 90%}.
- Surface estimated cost delta in the UI when users change prewarm or batch knobs (show % change vs baseline).
- Add a "burst simulator" in console that replays sampled session traces against the chosen knobs to show expected p90/p99 curves.

Open questions / TODOs:
- Need larger sweep across more shapes (multi-tenant interference, mixed-length tokens). Current numbers come from isolated harness. (JIRA-1420)
- Validate with production telemetry (10% sample) for 2 weeks before we ship SLO presets. Link: CONFLUENCE-TPR-774.
- UX: what language do we use to recommend prewarm levels to customers who must minimize cost? (scripting suggestions vs one-click)

Appendix: micro-observations and rough method notes
- Harness: 1000 simulated sessions for microburst (90% of traffic in 30s window), 10k queries total per run.
- Instance mix: A100-like profile for interactive group, A10G-like for background runs (not strictly hardware parity).
- Cost model: simple amortized reserved-capacity math + runtime token cost. We did not include egress or storage.
- Charts: ascii tables above are snapshots; full CSVs and plot notebooks are linked in PR.

Notes to self (informal):
- Marcus: grab 2 real tenant traces and run the batch sweep with int8 fallback logic; we need to capture p99 tail behavior when fallback triggers on hallucinations.
- Elena: would you prototype the console delta UI with the three presets and a slider for prewarm? I sketched a mock in figma link in PR description.

End of snapshot. This doc should be a short companion to the deeper bench notebooks — use it for product/console sync and drafting the public-facing one-pager later.
